analysis.one_liner: Repeals corporate tax breaks and subsidies and makes mining companies pay royalties on public-land minerals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 1999 with two cosponsors, the bill was referred to seven House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a set of federal subsidies and tax breaks for corporations: a tax exclusion for foreign sales corporations, ethanol fuel tax incentives, agricultural export promotion programs, tobacco price supports, the Advanced Technology Program, TVA appropriations, and federal funding of logging roads. It would also replace the 1872 Mining Law, requiring hardrock mining companies to pay an 8% royalty on minerals taken from public land, pay claim fees, post reclamation bonds, and clean up abandoned mine sites. All new revenue would go to deficit reduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop paying for export subsidies, fuel tax breaks, and below-market mining of public minerals; users of public lands and waters, who would gain from reclamation standards, reclamation bonds, and an abandoned-mine cleanup fund; and future budgets, since all revenue raised would be locked toward deficit reduction.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the foreign sales corporation tax exclusion and revises income-sourcing rules, ending tax benefits for exporters that shifted income abroad [S2][S3].
Repeals ethanol and alcohol fuel tax incentives, including excise exemptions and credits [S2][S3].
Repeals the Export Enhancement Program and Market Access Program and ends tobacco price supports and marketing quotas [S2][S3].
Ends federal funding of forest roads used principally for logging and codifies the elimination of purchaser road credits [S2][S3].

Replaces the 1872 Mining Law regime with an 8% royalty on locatable minerals, annual claim maintenance fees, exploration and operations permits, reclamation plans, financial assurance, and citizen suits for enforcement [S2][S3].
Creates an Abandoned Locatable Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund, funded by the new fees and royalties, to clean up mined lands that threaten public health, safety, and water [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Exporters using foreign sales corporations, ethanol producers, agribusiness exporters, tobacco growers, the logging industry, TVA, the Advanced Technology Program, and hardrock mining companies, which would for the first time pay royalties, fees, and reclamation costs on public-land mining.
analysis.who_pays_short: Miners, exporters, ethanol and tobacco interests

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledges that hardrock mining is capital-intensive and that royalties and fees must not discourage essential mining activity; new royalties, fees, and permitting could raise costs and reduce domestic mineral production [S3].
Eliminating the Advanced Technology Program and TVA appropriations cuts government-funded research and rural programs, not only corporate subsidies [S2][S3].

Repealing ethanol fuel incentives would raise costs for alcohol fuel producers and blenders, and the bill even imposes an 18.4-cents-per-gallon floor stocks tax on fuel alcohol held on January 1, 2000 [S3].
Ending tobacco price supports and quotas would eliminate a federal program that stabilized income for small tobacco growers, even as it removed a subsidy the public no longer wanted to fund [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's central trade is public money for private subsidies: it would raise revenue from exporters, ethanol blenders, and mining on public land while cutting programs that also serve some public purposes, like federal research grants and rural development. The strongest objection is that the new mining costs and the loss of price supports would fall partly on smaller operators, not just large corporations, and that repealing fuel tax incentives works against alternative fuels. On the other side, the bill directly addresses transfers the public pays for with no return, including royalty-free mining on federal land and abandoned mines left unreclaimed. The design is broad but internally consistent: every dollar raised is dedicated to deficit reduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to seven House committees and then to subcommittees, none of which ever reported it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Visclosky introduced the Corporate Responsibility Act of 1999 on April 15, 1999 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred the same day to seven committees: Ways and Means, Resources, Agriculture, Science, Banking and Financial Services, Budget, and Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S3][S5].
Between April 16 and April 30, 1999, it was referred to six subcommittees, and executive comment was requested from USDA and Interior [S5].
No committee reported the bill, and the House never voted on it; the last recorded action was the April 30, 1999 subcommittee referral [S1][S5].
The bill had only two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries receiving the subsidies were better off: hardrock mining companies continued to extract public-land minerals without paying a royalty, and the tax breaks, export programs, and logging-road funding the bill would have ended all remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Subsidy-receiving industries kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only support was one Democratic sponsor plus one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill would end the 1872 Mining Law regime that lets companies patent and mine public-land minerals without paying royalties, imposing an 8% royalty, claim fees, permits, and reclamation bonds instead. Their current arrangement costs the public revenue and leaves abandoned mines unreclaimed.

industries.industry: Multinational exporters using foreign sales corporations
industries.note: The bill would repeal the FSC tax exclusion, which lets exporters shield foreign-trade income from U.S. tax. The forgone revenue is made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.

The bill would repeal the alcohol fuel tax incentives, including excise exemptions and credits that subsidize ethanol blending. Ordinary motorists pay the difference through forgone highway-fund revenue.

The bill would repeal the Export Enhancement Program and Market Access Program and eliminate tobacco price supports and marketing quotas. These programs direct public funds to agricultural sellers rather than to public benefits.

industries.industry: Logging companies operating in national forests
industries.note: The bill would bar federal funding of logging roads and codify the end of purchaser road credits, under which taxpayers subsidized road construction that mainly benefited timber buyers.

The bill would end all TVA appropriations after September 30, 1999. TVA appropriations funded non-power programs, so cutting them removes a public subsidy but also eliminates some public services in the Tennessee Valley.
